title: Holy Texas
author: Lawrence Davidson
content:

Bang! Texas. Graffiti, Portland, Oregon. Photo: Jeffrey St. Clair.

I have been thinking about folks who are into one or another messianic
worldviews. This can be a secular or religious search for what is really a
false sense of certainty. Either way that need for certainty requires one to
think that history is foreordained and believe they hold the secret to
correctly predicting mankind’s future. The United States has several versions
of this obsession, among them Christian Fundamentalists and Christian
Nationalists.

**Who Are They?**

You can describe these fundamentalists and nationalists as Christian
absolutists. That is, anything the Bible (preferable the King James version)
says is absolutely true. You can trace their communities back to 18th century
America, but here I want to concentrate on the early 20th century.

In the first half of the 20th century, the fundamentalists were, by default,
both politically and socially influential. This was because in many sections
of the country (particularly the South) it was taken for granted that a
Biblical interpretation of history and morality was self-evident. Many state
legislatures, governors, town mayors and councilmen (not a lot of women in
office), followed this creed (at least in public). However, this broad
influence eroded in the multicultural and secularizing environment of evolving
large urban centers.

That change came to the surface in 1925 because of an event in Dayton,
Tennessee. There, “a high school teacher, John T. Scopes, was accused of
violating a Tennessee state law by teaching human evolution in a public
school.” While he was ultimately convicted and fined, the trial of Scopes was
a turning point in public opinion. In those multicultural urban areas (then
growing economically dominant), the Scopes trial seemed a demonstration of
Christian fundamentalism’s superstitious and anti-modern character. In the
decades following, many of the nation’s Christian fundamentalist communities
became more insular—seeking to isolate themselves from the corrupting effects
of a growing secular society.

This insularity lasted into the late 1970s. At that point in time an energetic
Baptist minister/televangelist named Jerry Falwell founded the Moral Majority.
The assertion of morality here was based on the assumption of the
fundamentalist creed that it knew God's mind. The majority assertion was an
attempt to make Falwell’s movement appear larger than it actually was. In any
case, Falwell was a talented organizer and the movement did grow, aligning
itself with various conservative social causes. Falwell threw his support
behind the Republican Party of Ronald Reagan and indeed helped Reagan become
president in 1980. The movement would inspire what is now the multifaceted
Christian right. In turn, the Christian right found another political hero in
Donald Trump. On Trump's coattails a slew of social reformers of Christian
persuasion came to office. And so, today we are faced with not only Christian
fundamentalists but also a parallel Christian nationalist campaign hoping to
politically capture the entire country and universalize the religious creed
that seemed to go into decline after the Scopes trial.

**Texas**

For someone of a secular background, someone who believes in the efficacy of
science to explain the world, Christian fundamentalism is an escape into
fantasy. Actually all religions are such an escape, though those that do not
have messianic and proselytizing characteristics are a safer, more
individually centered variety. The American brand of Christian fundamentalism
is, however, something else. It is on a “mission from God.”

Want an example? Let's take a look at Texas.

On Friday, June 26, 2026, the Republican-controlled Texas State Board of
Education voted 9 to 5 to approve a required reading list for public school
students that includes Bible stories. There will also be a new social science
program with Christian-inspired lessons on how the “meaning” of the stories
link to examples of great literature and U.S. history. This will be introduced
in a state that already requires copies of the Ten Commandments to be
displayed in all public school classrooms. Is this an effort to
institutionalize a fundamentalist form of Christianity through the mechanism
of public education? There are over 5 million public school students in Texas.

Here are some examples of those Bible stories:

> \+ At the elementary school level emphasis will be put on adventure stories
> wherein good guys appear to overcome bad guys, such as David and Goliath,
> Daniel in the Lion’s Den, and the story of Moses. Then, in the 5th grade,
> there is a transfer to the New Testament with passages about Jesus somehow
> made compatible with the prior stories.
>
> \+ Middle School students in the 6th and 7th grade will be required to take
> up Jesus’s teachings. The example given by the school board is the Sermon on
> the Mount.
>
> \+ At the High School level the emphasis goes back to the Old Testament
> where students will read, among other passages, the story of Adam and Eve
> and the Book of Job (I wonder how the teachers will rationalize that one).
> In an effort to show how this is all culturally relevant, the new approach
> requires that “these selections will be paired alongside works like Jane
> Austen’s Pride and Prejudice and books by Charles Dickens.” I think it would
> be fun to pair Jonah in the belly of the whale (“great fish”) with Moby
> Dick.

Here are a couple of questions to ask:

Except as a disguised proselytizing tool, does any of this make sense?
Approximately one-third of the public school students in Texas are not
Christian. They are Hindus, Muslims, Buddhists and a fair number of Jews—not
to mention a handful of closet atheists. As one interviewed teacher observed,
“I can say all day long, ‘Well, we’re teaching a theme, we’re teaching
symbolism,’ but they’re hearing, ‘This is a Bible story. We’re talking about
[somebody else’s] God.’”

What percentage of the country’s educated population actually believe the
rationalizations given in support of this curriculum? Rationalizations such
as, (1) “Supporters of the changes have argued that Judeo-Christian traditions
were fundamental to the nation’s founding and that should be reflected in the
public school curriculum.” In fact, most of the “Founding Fathers” were
deists. And, in 18th century America, the _fundamental_ thing Judeo-Christian
belief and the Bible were used to support was slavery. That would not change
until the abolitionists came along in the 19th century—a generation past the
time of the “founding.” (2) It is claimed that “these timeless works,
including Biblical passages, have shaped American culture and history, and
have influenced generations of thinkers, leaders, and citizens.” Well, is that
a good or bad thing? If these “timeless [religious] works” were seen as so
positively influential and convincing, why was there always a constitutional
barrier between church and state? The answer is that the “Founding Fathers”
were well aware of the bloody history of European states fused to one religion
or another. It continues today in several Muslim countries as well as in
Israel. Obviously this is a history unknown in the “great” state of Texas.

Finally, is any of this constitutional? Well, the U.S. Constitution forbids
(in the so-called Establishment Clause of the First Amendment) the federal __
government from "creating or officially favoring a national religion, and from
overly entangling itself in religious matters.” According to the decision of
the US Supreme Court in 1940, (based on the 14th Amendment which established
the supremacy of federal law) that disestablishment of religion applies to all
state governments. The Texas move, on the face of it, would seem to be an
effort, through its control of public education, to establish a brand of
Christianity as the religion favored by the state. Hence, it is
unconstitutional.

Will the Trump administration fulfill its role as defender of the Constitution
in this case? The Republicans, who control both the Texas state legislature
and the Board of Education, are all Trump supporters. In the last presidential
election, Trump carried the state with a 13.6% majority. Given Donald Trump's
dismal record of enforcing the Constitution along progressive lines, the
chances are pretty good that he will do nothing to enforce the “Establishment
Clause.” This puts the president himself in conflict with the Constitution,
and not for the first time.

**Conclusion**

Perhaps the most important point to consider is that historically,
fundamentalists/absolutists (be they of the religious or secular variety) have
always had a disastrous impact on society whenever they attain power. This
apparent inevitability stems from (1) their hard core belief that they have a
mission to direct history in a preset direction (2) and in carrying out that
mission, they suppress those who disagree particularly when the dissenters get
close to majority status. As far as I know, there is no historical example of
fundamentalists/absolutists in power operating in a way that is compatible
with democracy.

It is the power of the U.S. Constitution that can hold at bay the nation’s
Christian fundamentalist attempt to rule. How long will that last? These
ideologues now have a president that caters to their ambitions, and they are
likely to prosper as long as he does. Thus, if Trump ever conspires to
overturn the Constitution, the Christian fundamentalists can be expected to
back him.

This is what happens when you know no history or have been raised to replace
real history with myth. The Texas State Board of Education has taken the first
step in that direction.
